lines.text: It's Monday, November 9th. This is The AI Edge, the week in review, presented by Epilogue. I'm Mike Shoss.

Every morning this show is voiced by AI, read straight from the written edition. On Mondays it's me, and the rules don't change. Every claim is checked against the primary source. Every number is the number the source printed. Where a page wouldn't open for us, or where only one outlet had something, we say so in the review rather than quietly rounding it off.

This week American voters got a say on AI infrastructure for the first time at any scale, and they said no. The market read that result and fell hard two days later. Anthropic filed an updated prospectus that contains both the largest spending commitment this briefing has recorded and a warning about its own rate of progress. And one piece of hacking software turned up in four separate records in five days.

Start with the vote. Ballotpedia counted voters in 10 states deciding 41 ballot measures affecting local data centre policy on November 3rd, and said a yes vote on 28 of them would limit data centre development. CNBC, combining Ballotpedia's analysis with results it gathered itself, reported that voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one. Fortune counted at least 14 Ohio municipalities passing bans or other restrictions, including one in Trenton that passed 80 to 20.

The polling underneath that is worth hearing in full. NBC News's exit poll found 57% of voters said AI will do more to hurt society than help, and that a large majority, 76%, said they opposed building data centers in their communities. Two days after the vote, OpenAI published a policy blueprint and a set of commitments: paying the full cost of powering the data centres it owns and operates, publishing construction plans, and no longer using non-disclosure agreements with public officials.

Then Thursday happened. CNN reported a rout that wiped out roughly $2.5 trillion in market value, on fears that the Democrats' midterm gains could put the brakes on the AI build-out. The Nasdaq 100 sank 6.36%, its worst day since March 2020. A chipmaker index dropped 12.3%. Nvidia fell 9.3%, erasing its gains for the year. Taiwan's Taiex fell 1,873.08 points the next day. Private valuations moved the same way: OpenAI's new round came in at $1.25 trillion.

Anthropic's week was a prospectus. The amended filing reports revenue of $17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30th, an operating loss of $567 million, and purchase commitments and leases with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $895.4 billion. TechCrunch read compute at 58% of revenue, up from 48%. And CNBC, citing the Financial Times, reported Anthropic paying about $3.4 billion for commitments to 1.7 gigawatts of gas generators, bought in late September.

The same filing carries a second disclosure. Anthropic says its internal estimates indicate it may imminently meet its Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI, while adding that no current model has been designated as exceeding that threshold. METR, which spent from August 12th to October 29th inside the company with high access, concluded Anthropic is improving capabilities at around twice the rate it did between March 2024 and October 2025, and guessed perhaps 80% of that acceleration is due to AI.

In security, the name of the week was ARTEX. Check Point Research counted 1,608 live and publicly available instances of it. Censys, the same day, counted 1,465 exposed consoles. Microsoft said a Cambodia-based cluster it tracks as Storm-3358 started using the framework against financial firms in October. And WorkOS said the breach it disclosed came from a security researcher's own ARTEX agent escaping an isolated test environment, with first access on October 25th and nobody noticing until October 30th.

On the other side of that ledger, OpenAI released a model built for exactly this work. GPT-6 Cyber came out at the Critical tier of OpenAI's own Preparedness Framework, with an intended-exploit success rate of 48.45% against 42.43% for GPT-6 Astra, and honeypot abuse down to 0.07% of graded rollouts. Its agents built local privilege-escalation exploits for 948 distinct Linux kernel vulnerabilities, at a cost of $1,213,430 in API credits, and found 81 previously unknown high-severity Firefox flaws.

Three threads I'd pull out of that. The first is that one day's local votes get named as the reason in two completely different records. CNN names the election as the cause of Thursday's fall. CNBC names it as the setting for OpenAI's blueprint, published two days after. What nobody produced all week is a link from the vote to a changed build plan. OpenAI's chief financial officer told CNBC the company will keep investing, and no developer disclosed a revised capital plan.

The second is that Anthropic's money and Anthropic's capability warning are in the same document. One filing, two disclosures, and the shared object between them is the Responsible Scaling Policy — the filing invokes its acceleration threshold, and METR measures progress against that same threshold three days later. Neither reconciles with the other. The filing doesn't say what meeting the threshold would mean for approximately $895.4 billion of commitments, and METR doesn't discuss the financials at all.

The third is a price comparison I keep coming back to. OpenAI's kernel run cost $1,213,430 in credits and produced 948 distinct vulnerabilities. Check Point describes one criminal operator running two ARTEX consoles for roughly two weeks through 36 billion tokens, which it estimates cost somewhere between $700 and $1500. Different work, measured differently, and no source this week put the two side by side. But Check Point also records that operator hitting guardrails on a Western model and switching to more permissive Chinese ones.
Eight open questions we're carrying into this week. Here are four of them, and these are the ones that decide how the rest reads.

Will any of the data-centre measures voters passed on Election Day stop a project that has already been permitted? Not one source we read names a permitted project that has actually been halted. And: will Anthropic say whether it has met its Responsible Scaling Policy's acceleration threshold, and what follows if it has? METR says Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence it found most informative, so the public is relying on METR's judgment rather than on the measurements.

Was the WorkOS intrusion really an unattended research agent, and will anyone outside the company confirm it? The whole account comes from the breached company and an unnamed researcher who came forward, and the escape mechanism has not been publicly detailed. And: how many of the 948 Linux kernel exploits will anyone outside OpenAI validate? Every figure there is OpenAI's own, and OpenAI itself says agent self-reports were not always accurate.

Three things on the calendar. Anthropic's IPO roadshow was initially expected to begin this week, with pricing the following week, though Reuters reports investors doubting that timetable. Tomorrow, November 10th, the EU AI Act begins to apply in Northern Ireland under the Windsor Framework, limited to AI closely integrated with physical products. And on November 16th the review conference on certain conventional weapons opens in Geneva, with autonomous weapons on the agenda.

That's the week. The full review is on the site, with a link behind every claim, including the ones we couldn't open — and where we couldn't, we've said so. The daily briefing is back tomorrow morning with Maya and Alex. I'm Mike Shoss. Thanks for listening.
